newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Clinton aide Morris says polls replace hunches.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Clinton aide Morris says polls replace hunches.

text.p: Political consultant Dick Morris, dumped last summer as President Clinton's campaign adviser after a sex scandal, Monday defended Clinton's heavy reliance on polling during the 1996 presidential campaign.

Morris, on a promotional tour for his book about the Clinton campaign, took part in a forum at the National Press Club on the role of campaign strategists in elections, where he defended polling and took issue with critics' charges that Clinton was driven by surveys rather than principles.

"I think that Bill Clinton did not use polling to decide what to be for," Morris said. "He used polling to replace hunching -- which is what politicians had to use before there was polling, to figure out how to get a majority of the people to support what he wanted to support."

In his book "Behind the Oval Office: Winning the Presidency in the Nineties," the long-time adviser to Clinton said polls bonded their relationship that dated back to Clinton's days as governor of Arkansas.

"From the beginning of our relationship in 1977, polls have been my common frame of reference with Bill Clinton," Morris wrote. He said Clinton used polls almost daily as if they were "giant windsocks" to test political wind directions.

While he worked with Clinton in the White House as his political adviser in the last campaign, snap polls were taken on many subjects including where Clinton should go on vacation and what ties the president wore, Morris wrote.

Morris was forced out as Clinton's top consultant hours before the president was to give his accepance speech for renomination at the Democratic convention in Chicago after a tabloid reported Morris had a relationship with a prostitute.
